passage:
Friday
At 7:40 this morning Keerthana posted: "I AM LITERALLY DYING!!!!!! WORST DAY OF MY ENTIRE LIFE" with three crying faces and a skull. My heart jumped. Keerthana's grandmother has been ill, so for about ten seconds I was really scared. Then I remembered she also wrote "I AM DEAD" when the canteen ran out of chilli potatoes. Still. I messaged her privately: "hey, actual dying or canteen dying? 🙂" She replied, "CANTEEN LEVEL. I spilled ink on my white uniform on the bus. Everyone saw 😩" Then a second message: "thanks for checking tho Pema. Nani's okay, she's home now." So maybe 20 percent real feeling and 80 percent show for the class group. I do this too. Last week I wrote "BEST DAY EVER!!!" about a samosa. Maybe typing needs a volume knob. Taking my spare cardigan to school tomorrow in case the ink hasn't come out.

qa.q: What did Keerthana spill on her uniform?
qa.a: Keerthana spilled ink on her white uniform on the bus.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when the 7:40 post appeared?
qa.a: Pema felt a jolt of fear, knowing Keerthana's grandmother had been ill, before remembering how often Keerthana exaggerates; the worry was real for those ten seconds.

qa.q: What small step helped Pema read the post right?
qa.a: A quick private check, 'actual dying or canteen dying?', got the real meaning in one reply instead of guessing from capitals and emojis. 🙂

qa.q: How much of the post was real feeling for Keerthana?
qa.a: The ink was genuinely embarrassing for Keerthana, but the capitals and emojis were mostly performance for the class group, as 'CANTEEN LEVEL' shows.

grounding: It shows capital letters and dramatic emojis mixing real feeling with performance online, and a quick private check clarifying the tone.

passage: Yogesh beta, you think your mother never slammed a door? Sit, and let your Hansa Nani tell you about Meena at fifteen. One Sunday she laughed so hard at your Nana's joke about the goat that she fell off the charpai. Twenty minutes later she was snapping at me because I had moved her bangles. By lunch she was crying over something she couldn't even name, face in the pillow. I wanted to shout, "Which Meena am I talking to?" Your Nana stopped me. He said, "She's tired. She was up reading till two again." So we tried something. No arguments after dinner, lights out at ten for everyone, even your Nana with his radio. And every evening I sat on her bed for five minutes, not asking anything, just there. The storms didn't stop. But they got smaller, and she started telling me about them. Now you slam doors, and she's the one sitting on your bed. That's how it goes.

qa.q: What did Meena laugh at that Sunday?
qa.a: Meena laughed at Nana's joke about the goat.

qa.q: What might young Meena have been feeling across that Sunday?
qa.a: Meena swung from amusement to irritation to a sadness she couldn't name, likely made worse by tiredness from reading till two.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped Meena's moods settle?
qa.a: The family chose calm routines, no arguments after dinner and lights out at ten, and Hansa sat quietly on Meena's bed each evening, which made the storms smaller.

qa.q: What did Nana see that Hansa didn't at first?
qa.a: Nana saw tiredness from late-night reading behind the swings, so he stopped Hansa from shouting.

grounding: It shows a teenager swinging from laughing to irritable to tearful within hours, and patient consistency, sleep and gentle presence supporting balance.

passage: The auto was stuck in the flooded underpass for forty minutes, rain drumming on the canvas roof, and Mohit had said exactly one word since his father, Shankar, picked him up from cricket camp. "Fine." "Selection list came out today, na?" Shankar tried. Mohit shrugged. "Yeah. Not in. Whatever. It's fine." He stared at a scooter half floating in the brown water outside. Shankar noticed the kit bag still zipped, the gloves Mohit always hung off it tucked away inside. He wanted to ask twenty questions. But the driver was listening, the horns were deafening, and Mohit's jaw was set. So Shankar only said, "Okay. If it stops being fine, or even if it stays fine, I'm up late tonight. Chai at eleven, if you want company." Mohit didn't answer. At 11:10 the kitchen light was on, and Mohit was standing in the doorway in his socks. "Can I have the ginger one?"

qa.q: How long was the auto stuck in the underpass?
qa.a: It was stuck for forty minutes.

qa.q: What might Mohit have been feeling behind 'Whatever. It's fine'?
qa.a: Mohit was probably disappointed and hurt at not being selected, as the hidden gloves hint, but played it down to avoid drama in front of the driver; he may also simply have been tired.

qa.q: How did Shankar leave the door open without pushing?
qa.a: He held back his questions in the noisy auto and offered a clear, no-pressure time to talk, chai at eleven, whether things were fine or not.

qa.q: What was the ride like for Shankar?
qa.a: Shankar was concerned and itching to ask questions, but chose patience because the place was noisy and public.

grounding: It shows a teenager playing down disappointment with a shrug and 'fine', and a trusted adult leaving the door open instead of pressing.

passage: At the kasba school's annual sports day, the ground was still slick from the night's rain. Ujjwal was running the last leg of the relay, the whole school lined up along the rope, when his foot went out from under him and he slid three metres on his back through the mud, baton still in his fist. For a second there was total silence. Then Ujjwal sat up and laughed. Loudly, head thrown back, waving the muddy baton like a flag. Everyone laughed with him. "He's so confident," someone near Arohi said. "I'd have died." Arohi wasn't so sure. His laugh went on a beat too long, and his ears were bright red under the mud. Later, rinsing his shirt at the handpump, Ujjwal said to her without looking up, "If I didn't laugh first, they'd have laughed at me instead." Then, quieter: "Also, honestly, I was just glad nothing was broken."

qa.q: What was Ujjwal holding when he slid?
qa.a: Ujjwal still had the baton in his fist.

qa.q: What feelings might Ujjwal's loud laugh have been covering?
qa.a: Most likely embarrassment and a fear of being laughed at, shown by the red ears and a laugh that went on too long; it was also partly relief that nothing was broken.

qa.q: How could Arohi support Ujjwal?
qa.a: Arohi could keep checking in quietly, as at the handpump, and avoid bringing up the fall in front of others, since the laugh was protection.

qa.q: Why might the classmate near Arohi read the laugh as confidence?
qa.a: From a distance a loud laugh and a waved baton look carefree, so that classmate missed the red ears and the too-long laugh.

grounding: It shows a teenager laughing loudly after a public slip, others reading it as confidence, while it covered embarrassment, fear of mockery and relief.

passage:
Ira: hey. random q. that joke Karan made in class about your voice cracking
Manoj: lol yeah
Manoj: it was funny 😅
Ira: you laughed. not saying it wasn't funny to you. just checking, cos you went quiet after
Manoj: I'm fine
Ira: ok. I believe you if you say so. offer stays open tho
(ten minutes later)
Manoj: ok it kind of sucked. it's the third time this week
Manoj: if I don't laugh they'll say I can't take a joke
Ira: that makes sense. the laugh was a shield
Ira: want me to sit next to you tomorrow? and if it keeps happening we can tell Ms Rao together
Manoj: yeah. sitting next to me would help
Ira: done. and your voice is fine btw

qa.q: How many times had the joke happened this week?
qa.a: It was the third time this week.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when writing 'it was funny'?
qa.a: Manoj was most likely hurt and embarrassed, using the laugh as a shield so as not to look weak; part of the joke may still have seemed funny in the moment.

qa.q: What did Ira do that made it easier to talk?
qa.a: Ira asked privately, didn't insist Manoj was hurt, accepted 'I'm fine' while leaving the offer open, and then suggested concrete support. 🤍

qa.q: What might Karan have missed by seeing only the laugh?
qa.a: Karan probably took the laugh as a sign the joke was harmless, missing that it was the third time and that Manoj went quiet afterwards.

grounding: It shows a teenager laughing off a hurtful joke to avoid looking weak, and a peer following up privately without assuming and offering support.

passage: My first month doing my master's in Osaka, I was convinced my lab partner, Aoi, disliked me. When I presented my data at the Thursday meeting, my friends back home would have been nodding, interrupting, going "arre wah!" Aoi just sat very still, hands folded, face almost blank, and said "Thank you" at the end. I went back to my desk feeling like I'd bombed. Lakshmi, from Chennai, who had been in the lab three years, laughed when I told her. "Raghav, my grandmother keeps that exact face at weddings. For her it means respect. But don't turn one person into a whole country. Just ask her." So I did, awkwardly, by the coffee machine: "Was my presentation okay? I couldn't tell." Aoi looked surprised. "It was very clear. I was concentrating so I would not miss anything. Your graph of the enzyme curve, can you send it?" I sent it that afternoon.

qa.q: What did Aoi ask Raghav to send?
qa.a: Aoi asked for the graph of the enzyme curve.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel after the Thursday presentation?
qa.a: Raghav felt deflated and anxious, sure the talk had bombed because Aoi's face stayed almost blank; Raghav was reading home expectations onto that face.

qa.q: What advice from Lakshmi helped, and why?
qa.a: Lakshmi pointed out that a still face can mean respect, warned against turning one person into a whole country, and said to ask, which got a direct answer.

qa.q: What did the still face mean for Aoi?
qa.a: For Aoi it meant concentrating so as not to miss anything, and she actually found the presentation very clear.

grounding: It shows a young adult abroad misreading a colleague's restrained face as coldness, and asking directly instead of relying on a stereotype.

passage: During my first remote internship last summer, I learned not to trust a frozen face. I was presenting my market survey to my supervisor, Hansa, over a video call from my hostel room, and halfway through the slides her face froze mid-frown: eyebrows pulled together, mouth slightly open, as if I'd said something unforgivable. The audio kept going for a second, then cut. My heart sank. I kept talking to the frozen frown, getting faster and more apologetic, adding "but of course I could redo this" to every slide. When she reconnected, she said, "Sorry, Gopika, the power went off here. What did I miss after slide four?" I almost laughed with relief. Now I do something simple. If a face looks unhappy on a call, I ask: "Did that make sense, or is the connection bad?" Last week Hansa frowned again. I asked. "Oh, I'm concentrating," she said. "Your numbers are good. Keep going."

qa.q: What had cut off Hansa's call?
qa.a: The power went off at Hansa's end.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling while talking to the frozen frown?
qa.a: Gopika felt anxious and increasingly apologetic, sure the frown meant disapproval, when it was really a frozen frame from a power cut.

qa.q: What habit does Gopika now use on calls?
qa.a: When a face looks unhappy, Gopika asks, 'Did that make sense, or is the connection bad?', checking verbally instead of reading a paused face.

qa.q: What did the frown mean for Hansa the second time?
qa.a: Hansa was simply concentrating, and she thought the numbers were good.

grounding: It shows a young adult misreading a frozen frown on a video call as disapproval, and learning to check in verbally instead.

passage: I share a college flat with Dilnaz and Ganga, so I was on the sofa when Dilnaz gave Ganga her birthday present: a watercolour of the pond in Ganga's village, which Dilnaz had worked on for two weeks. Ganga said, "Oh wow, thank you!" and smiled. It was a nice smile, but only her mouth moved, and it lasted about a second before she leaned the painting against the wall. Dilnaz's face flickered. Later, in the kitchen, Dilnaz whispered to me, "She hated it. Did you see? Mouth only." I honestly couldn't tell. Ganga is quiet about everything; she smiled the same way when she got her exam results. That night I saw Ganga sitting alone with the painting on her knees, touching the corner with the lotus, and her whole face was soft. I told Dilnaz. The next morning the painting was up on Ganga's wall, and Ganga said, "It's exactly the colour at dawn."

qa.q: How long had Dilnaz worked on the painting?
qa.a: Dilnaz had worked on it for two weeks.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when she whispered 'She hated it'?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt hurt and anxious, reading the quick mouth-only smile as dislike; but that smile was only a rough clue, since Ganga smiles quietly about everything.

qa.q: What would be a wiser way for Dilnaz to read Ganga's reaction?
qa.a: Compare it with Ganga's usual quiet smile and simply ask, rather than judging from one brief expression.

qa.q: How did Ganga seem to feel about the painting later?
qa.a: Alone with it that night, Ganga looked soft and touched, then hung it up and said it was exactly the colour at dawn.

grounding: It shows a young adult reading a brief mouth-only smile as polite dislike when it was a quiet genuine one, so the cue works only as a rough clue.

passage: In her first month studying in Seoul, Wanjiru smiled at everyone the way she did at home in Nairobi: the bus driver, the woman at the kimbap stall, a man on the subway. The man looked away fast, and a teenager nearby stared as if she had done something strange. Wanjiru's cheeks went hot. Then, in the campus cafeteria, her classmate Soo-ah bumped her tray and knocked Wanjiru's soup into her lap. Soo-ah bowed quickly, and she was smiling. Smiling! Wanjiru felt a flash of anger. Was this funny? Later Soo-ah found her in the library, eyes worried. "I'm so sorry about the soup. When I'm embarrassed I smile, I can't help it. My mother does the same." Wanjiru laughed, surprised. "At home that smile would look like you were laughing at me." "And here," Soo-ah said, "smiling at the bus driver might look like you know him." They swapped rules over coffee: two people, not two countries.

qa.q: What did Soo-ah knock into Wanjiru's lap?
qa.a: Soo-ah knocked Wanjiru's soup into her lap.

qa.q: What was Wanjiru feeling when Soo-ah smiled after the spill?
qa.a: Wanjiru felt a flash of anger, reading the smile as mockery; it turned out to come from Soo-ah's embarrassment.

qa.q: What helped the two of them understand each other?
qa.a: Soo-ah came back to apologise and explain the smile, and they swapped their own habits over coffee instead of judging each other.

qa.q: What was the spill like for Soo-ah?
qa.a: Soo-ah was embarrassed and worried, smiling out of that embarrassment, and later sought Wanjiru out to say sorry.

grounding: It shows a student in a new city finding that smiling at strangers reads differently there, and a smile covering embarrassment being misread until they talk.

passage: Harsha, you're worried about your forehead in tomorrow's interview? Then let your old colleague Vishal tell you something. My first interview, at the bank, I was so nervous that my forehead folded into three deep lines and stayed there. I was thinking hard, that's all. Afterwards the panel head told my uncle I seemed "irritated with the questions". Irritated! I was terrified. Before the next interview I practised in front of the mirror: when a question interested me, I let my eyebrows lift a little, and before answering I took one breath and smoothed my forehead. Small thing, but the second panel wrote that I seemed "engaged". Years later I sat on interview panels myself. When a young candidate's forehead was knotted up, I remembered that boy at the bank and told the others, "That's effort, not attitude." So practise a little, yes. But don't hate your forehead. It's only working hard.

qa.q: Where was Vishal's first interview?
qa.a: Vishal's first interview was at the bank.

qa.q: What was young Vishal feeling when that forehead folded into three lines?
qa.a: Vishal was terrified and thinking hard, not irritated as the panel head believed; the furrowed brow showed anxiety and effort.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed how the second panel saw Vishal?
qa.a: Practising in the mirror to let the eyebrows lift when interested and to smooth the forehead with a breath before answering made Vishal come across as 'engaged'.

qa.q: How did the first panel head read the furrowed forehead?
qa.a: The panel head read it as irritation with the questions, missing that it was nervous effort.

grounding: It shows a young adult learning to lift the brows for interest and smooth a nervous furrow in interviews, and an interviewer later remembering a tense forehead may only signal effort.
